items.prompt: Which of these is a magnetic material?
hints: Think about what a magnet can pick up.
Many nails are made of it.
items.explanation: Iron is a magnetic material.

items.prompt: What are the two ends of a magnet called?

options.text: the north pole and the south pole

items.explanation: A magnet has a north pole and a south pole.

items.prompt: An iron nail is a magnetic ___, not a magnet.
hints: It is attracted by a magnet.
items.explanation: Iron is a magnetic material. It is attracted to magnets but is not a magnet unless it is magnetised.

items.prompt: What is the difference between a magnet and a magnetic material?

options.text: A magnetic material always attracts other materials.
A magnet has its own magnetic force, but a magnetic material is only attracted to magnets.

hints: A magnet can attract and repel.
A magnetic material is only attracted.
items.explanation: A magnet has its own magnetic force. A magnetic material is attracted by a magnet but is not a magnet itself.

items.prompt: Which of these will a magnet NOT attract?
items.explanation: Copper is a metal but it is not magnetic.

items.prompt: Two magnets are held with their north poles close together. What happens?
hints: North and north are like poles.
items.explanation: Like poles repel, so two north poles push each other away.

items.prompt: Which statement about magnetic forces is true?

options.text: They only work when the objects touch.
options.why: Magnetic forces act across a gap.

options.text: They can act without the objects touching.

hints: A magnet can pick up a paper clip without touching it.
Gravity also works across a gap.
It is a force that acts over a distance.
items.explanation: Magnetic forces act over a distance, so a magnet can attract a nearby object without touching it.

items.prompt: Sort each object into magnetic or not magnetic.
hints: Wood, plastic and glass are not.
Try to remember which metals work.
items.explanation: Iron and steel objects are magnetic. Plastic, wood and glass are not.

items.prompt: A student tests two magnets. Magnet A picks up 12 paper clips and magnet B picks up 5. Which statement is true?

options.text: Magnet B is stronger than magnet A.
Magnet A is stronger than magnet B.

hints: More paper clips means more strength.
items.explanation: Magnet A picks up more paper clips, so it is stronger.

items.prompt: Magnet A holds 12 paper clips and magnet B holds 5. How many more paper clips does magnet A hold?
hints: Take the smaller number from the larger.
items.explanation: 12 − 5 = 7. Magnet A holds 7 more paper clips.

items.prompt: A magnet picks up a paper clip from 2 cm away but not from 6 cm away. What does this show?

options.text: The magnet only works up to 6 cm in water.
The magnetic force gets weaker with distance.
The paper clip stops being magnetic.
options.why: The force just gets too weak.

hints: The pull at 6 cm is too small.
items.explanation: Magnetic forces get weaker as distance grows, so the magnet works at 2 cm but not 6 cm.

items.prompt: How can a student compare the strength of two magnets?

options.why: Weight does not show magnetic strength.

options.text: Count how many paper clips each can hold.

options.why: Size does not always show strength.

hints: Count what each can pick up.
items.explanation: A stronger magnet can pick up more paper clips, so counting them is a fair test.

items.prompt: Which of these will a magnet attract?
hints: Think about which metals are iron-based.
items.explanation: A magnet attracts iron and steel. It does not attract aluminium or copper.

items.prompt: Which pair will attract each other?

options.text: a north pole and a south pole

items.explanation: Opposite poles attract and like poles repel.

items.prompt: Magnets and gravity are both forces that can act over a ___.
hints: They do not need to touch.
items.explanation: Both magnetic force and gravity can act over a distance.

items.prompt: A magnet is placed under a sheet of card with iron filings on top. The filings move. What does this show?

options.text: The magnetic force can act through the card.

options.why: Filings are tiny bits of iron.

hints: The magnet does not touch the filings.
The force passes through the card.
items.explanation: The force goes through the card, so it acts over a distance.

items.prompt: A paper clip is held up by a magnet and a second clip hangs from the first. Why does this happen?

options.text: The two clips are glued together.
The first clip becomes a temporary magnet.
The second clip is lighter than air.
options.why: It is not lighter than air.

hints: A magnet can make iron act like a magnet.
The effect stops when the magnet is removed.
The first clip attracts the second.
items.explanation: A magnetic material near a magnet can become magnetised for a short time, so the first clip attracts the second.

items.prompt: Which is the fairest way to compare two magnets?

options.text: Use big clips for one and small clips for the other.
options.why: That changes more than one thing.

options.text: Use the same paper clips and place each magnet at the same distance.
Test one in the sun and one in the shade.
options.why: The Sun does not matter here.

items.explanation: In a fair test only the magnet changes. The clips and the distance stay the same.

items.prompt: A magnet picks up 10 clips when new, but only 6 after being dropped many times. What is the best conclusion?
hints: Hitting a magnet can weaken it.
items.explanation: It holds fewer clips than before, so it has become weaker.

items.prompt: Why does a fridge magnet stick to a steel fridge door but not to a wooden cupboard?

options.text: Steel is a magnetic material and wood is not.

hints: The door is made of steel.
items.explanation: The magnet is attracted to the steel, which is magnetic. Wood is not magnetic.

items.prompt: True or false: A magnet can attract a magnetic object without touching it.
hints: Does a paper clip jump to a magnet?
It does not need to touch.
Magnetic force works at a distance.
items.explanation: Magnetic forces act at a distance, so the force can reach across a small gap.

items.prompt: True or false: Everything made of metal is a magnet.
items.explanation: Most metals are not magnets and many are not even magnetic. A magnet is an object that attracts iron and can repel other magnets.

items.prompt: True or false: The magnetic force gets weaker as the distance from the magnet grows.
hints: Is the pull stronger up close?
items.explanation: The farther away an object is, the weaker the pull.

items.prompt: True or false: Any object that a magnet attracts is a magnet itself.
hints: Does an iron nail push away a magnet?
A magnet can attract and repel.
items.explanation: Many things are attracted but are not magnets, such as an iron nail. They are magnetic materials, and a real magnet can also repel another magnet.
